title: Wilderness Basketball
speaker: Kusho Terry Thompson
summary: Kusho Terry Thompson tells the story of Kusho's 24-hour solo during the 2010 Mountains and Rivers hiking retreat on Mount Baker, which Kusho reads from notes written right after coming down, after a detour through basketball in Indiana, Kansas, and North Carolina. Alone in a meadow, Kusho sits with insects, bites from mosquitoes, and a line from the Heart Sutra about having no fear, then watches mites gang up on one and kill it. The sight leaves Kusho doubting that cruelty in nature can change. Rain on Kusho's tent settles Kusho, and a dream that ends on a basketball court leaves Kusho thinking Kusho should enjoy the game.

sentences.text: Thanks everyone for being here.
It's my first talk and I drew the Lucky Chant book.
Has anybody else ever gotten this?
Or do we have many of these?
I don't know.
It starts on page 10 and the table of contents is in the middle.
So if this is the only one of its kind, I feel either blessed or something really bad is about to happen.
I also coincidentally have 10 pages of notes.
So maybe that argues I should shuffle them or toss them and just talk.
I've always actually envisioned that my first talk would be sitting silently and saying nothing, like that old story of the Buddha doing the same and then raising the flower at the end.
But that would be a little presumptuous, I think.
I don't have an understanding of what that means myself, so I couldn't really talk about that.
Or not talk about that.
It's odd that I give presentations in my work.
That's a large part of what I do, and I don't get nervous doing that.
I've talked to rooms filled with large crowds of people.
Yet here I am with friends, very nervous.
You can probably feel my heartbeat on the other side of the room.
So I'm curious as to why that is.
I know, Tim, you don't seem to get nervous when you do talks.
But maybe it's because I know a lot about web accessibility.
I'm totally comfortable with the content when I'm up in front of an audience talking about that topic.
And when it comes to Zen, even though I've been at this for a while, I don't really feel like I know anything.
Or another way to say that is I know nothing.
Either those aren't the same or maybe they are the same.
I don't know anything, or I know nothing.
I was asked today to talk about my experience on the recent Mountains and Rivers retreat, where I spent 24 hours on a solo retreat in addition to doing the regular retreat, which I'll talk about.
And on that retreat, particularly in that 24-hour period, nothing happened.
So maybe I am qualified to talk about that.
I don't normally read my talks.
I normally wing it.
But as I mentioned, I've got 10 pages of notes, and pretty much I wrote the whole thing out.
I did this after we got back from the retreat, most of it, just because it felt fresh.
And it was going to be a while.
I was going to get back into civilization, and that was going to corrupt the mindset that I had at that time.
So I wanted to capture what I was feeling at that time.
I actually hadn't touched it much until just this week, when I started looking at it again.
It hasn't changed much.
I still have vivid memories of what happened there, and I stand behind everything that I wrote down at that time.
So I am going to read through what I wrote after returning from the wilderness.
But before I do that, I want to talk a bit about basketball.
That relates to my life and Zen practice.
It may seem like an odd fit, and it probably is.
But it may, may fit.
And for those of you who turn off immediately when you hear anything sports related, please bear with me.
It goes all the way back to the beginning, in New Castle, Indiana.
Bob Penny, who put on or leads, the Mountains and Rivers retreat, has for ten years now.
He's not able to be here tonight, and he really regretted that.
But he is either in Indiana now or on his way to Indiana with work.
So there is some irony there, some connection.
I grew up in Indiana, in a little town called New Castle, which is home to the world's largest high school field house.
The town has 20,000 people in it, and the field house seats 10,000.
On any given Friday or Saturday night when the men's basketball team is playing, it's a sellout.
So half the town goes to the basketball games.
It's a cliché to say this, but in Indiana basketball very much is a religion with a solid following, particularly in New Castle.
And I counted myself among those followers.
I went to college at Purdue, which is also in Indiana, and my friends and I had season tickets to watch the Boilermakers play basketball.
We never missed a game.
At Purdue, I majored in psychology and minored in philosophy and took classes on Eastern religion.
So that was really my first formal exposure to Buddhism and to other Eastern religions.
One of my professors was in fact Buddhist and sat full lotus as he lectured to us each day.
I really admired that, and it captivated me, and I became very interested.
After graduating, I relocated to Lawrence, Kansas, which is a college town about the same size as Bellingham and is home to the University of Kansas.
Conveniently, Kansas, like Indiana, was a land of basketballists.
The game was in fact invented by James Naismith, who was the first coach at KU.
And in 1987, which is when I relocated there, I pretty quickly discovered the Kansas Zen Center, which is a residential center in the Rinzai school.
I attended an introduction to Zen class one night there and never turned back.
That was also Danny Manning's senior year with the Kansas Jayhawks, and in 1988 Kansas won the national championship.

I remember how surprised I was when I showed up at an overflowing Big Six sports bar in the basement of the historic Eldridge Hotel downtown for the championship game and discovered at the front table, right in front of the big screen, all these people I'd been sitting with, bald-headed Zen monks from the center.
Just like everybody else there, they were all jumping up and cheering and giving each other high fives throughout the game.
That was a real eye-opener for me.
I had grown to know them sitting silently, yet here they were enjoying basketball at the same level that I was.
After 12 years in Lawrence, I moved to North Carolina, where I lived in the country halfway between Durham and Chapel Hill.
These two towns and their respective universities are home to the fiercest rivalry in college basketball.
Roy Williams, the head coach of Kansas during the majority of my 12 years there, had gotten his start as an assistant coach at North Carolina in Chapel Hill.
And after I moved there, so did Roy, to become North Carolina's head coach.
So there are all these incredible connections.
Chapel Hill is also home to the Chapel Hill Zen Center, which, like our own Red Cedar Zen Center Zen community, is in Suzuki Roshi's San Francisco Zen lineage.
I found the style and form there to be a bit more relaxed than what I'd started with in Kansas, and I liked that and began to practice regularly in the Soto tradition.
I've never turned back since then.
In 2001, my family and I moved to Washington.
That was to be closer to mountains and waters and family.
I immediately discovered the Bellingham Dharma Hall and this Zen community.
There didn't seem to be a whole lot of basketball fervor here compared to what I was used to.
But when I attended my first sesshin at Samish Island, those of you that have been there know what I'm about to say: I knew I belonged.
The zendo at Samish Island is a basketball court.
The altar with the Buddha sits at center court.
It really seemed perfect.
In 2000, the year before I relocated, Bob Penny organized the first, I believe that was the first, Mountains and Rivers, or Mountains and Waters, which is it, Rivers?
Hiking retreats.
I didn't attend that one because I was still in North Carolina, but I attended the second one, which was in 2002, I think.
I figured that out, that there was a year off, 2001.
Bob gave a talk a couple of months ago prior to the September retreat, and that's up on the website, redcedarzen.org, if folks didn't attend that and would like to listen to it.
He talked a lot about the background of the retreat, so I won't go into great depth about all of that.
But this past year marked the 10th anniversary of that retreat, and I've gone on nine of those, all but that first one.
The hike goes something like this.
I'll just give you the abridged version since Bob gave you more detail.
It starts on Thursday night when we sit in a cedar grove at Hawk Meadow Farm, which is Bob's place.
I know many of you have joined us for that, and I appreciate that.
Then that night there's a sweat lodge, and many of you have joined us for that as well.
Both of these things are open to anybody, including those that don't go on the longer hiking retreat.
The sweat lodge is an opportunity to cleanse ourselves in a Native American tradition and state our intentions for the hike.
It's a very powerful experience.
Then Friday we get up early.
We pack up, we have breakfast, and we head to the trailhead, which is on the south side of Mount Baker.

Late Friday morning, or early Friday afternoon, depending on how punctual we are, we hike eight or so miles, give or take, through old-growth forest, feeling the soft earth beneath our feet as we step.

It's one foot in front of the other, left and right, left and right, walking silently and listening to the birds or the rain or the wind or just listening to the deep penetrating silence of the forest.
Maybe we're elsewhere, listening to our thoughts or listening to, as I often do, the song that has found its way into my consciousness, accompanying the rhythm of my footsteps.
I've gotten pretty good at letting those sorts of distractions come and go and just being fully present as I walk, which is one of the reasons I've embraced hiking as a practice.
Bob mentioned in his recent talk that he came to hiking and backpacking first and Zen second.
The same is true for me.
I've always found that with hiking and backpacking, life is simple.
There's really nothing to do but walk and sit and listen and eat when you're hungry and drink when you're thirsty, sleep when night arrives.
At a traditional Zen retreat, all you possess, traditionally, are your robes and your bowls.
On a backpacking trip, it's pretty much the same.
All you possess is the stuff that you can fit in your backpack, whatever that may be.
And if you can make do with less, then life is easier.
Travel light.
There are no distractions in the wilderness.
It's just you and nature and plenty of time to get reacquainted.
So we arrive at base camp in the late afternoon.
We set up camp and we prepare and eat an informal evening meal.
There's a primitive three-sided hut in the base camp that we use as a zendo.
We set up an altar inside.
That's where we do most of our practice, and we settle in for evening zazen and kinhin.
At the end of the day, under the glow of a single candle or maybe the moon or a blanket of stars or the faint red remnants of the sunset over the Twin Sisters range, we chant the refuges in Pali.

I always get the sense that our voices are rising up from that hut in the meadow, rising up into the mountains and sky and somehow bringing some relief or some benefit to someone, somewhere who desperately needs that.
On Saturday morning, we arise.
We have morning zazen and a formal silent breakfast.
Then Bob leads each one of us to various sites that he's selected for our solos.
For the rest of the morning, which I believe is about two to three hours, we have time and space, each of us, to be alone with nature.
This year, for the first time, Bob invited me to do an extended solo.
So when the traditional two to three hour solo had ended, Bob made the rounds and picked up each person and escorted them back to the zendo and the meadow.
They sat another round of zazen, had lunch, then broke silence and had an informal afternoon for day hiking.
Usually during that time, we either go up to the fire lookout on Park Butte or over to the railroad grade, just a glacier moraine looking out over the south side of Mount Baker.
This year I understand that you guys opted for Park Butte.
And then the group returns for an informal dinner, followed by regular evening practice, ending again with the refuges and Pali.
So this year, while my comrades were doing all this, I remained at my solo site roughly 24 hours until Bob returned to pick me up after the group's first period of morning zazen on Sunday morning.
So what happened during my solo?
This is the part where I just sit.
Well, going in, I wondered what to expect.
I considered for a while whether I should try to attain something or do anything special in my practice at all.
I talked to Tim about that.
I talked to Bob about that.
But generally, we all agreed that it's probably best to expect nothing.
I considered my return as well.
When I came down from the mountain to join the group, what was that experience going to be like?
I knew there was time allocated to talk about what I had just experienced.
I imagined that I would be glowing.
Charlton Heston has a new hairstyle when he comes down off of the mountain.
That wasn't going to happen.
Or maybe I would just come back and report that nothing had happened.
Well, I wouldn't say that nothing happened in my spot.
Maybe superficially, if I hadn't been paying attention, I might describe the scene there as nothing.
It was just a silent meadow.
There really wasn't anything spectacular happening there.
There was nothing to do there.
It was, however, quite a meadow.
Bob has a real knack for picking spots.
There were several small creeks meandering through it.
To the west, I had a great view of the Sisters and to the northwest, the Black Buttes.
On all other sides, my meadow was surrounded by a thin ribbon of forest, then talus fields expanding upward toward some pretty spectacular cliff faces.
This year we had a more or less constant threat of rain.
So the first thing I did was find some relatively high flat ground to pitch a tent, just in case it was needed.
Then I found a spot in the meadow near the junction of two creeks and I sat and watched and listened.
Almost immediately I discovered that this was no quiet meadow.
Right in front of me there was constant motion.
Dozens, maybe hundreds of species of insects all scurrying or flying around, some fast, some slow.

Some, like ants and beetles, seemed to be on a mission, in a frantic hurry to get somewhere, while others, like a lone bee and a lone spider and another flying insect with long narrow wings and long antennae that I couldn't identify, seemed to be joining me in Zazen.
They just sat there for a very long time with me, and I really felt like they were aware that I was practicing Zazen and they were joining me in that practice.
Bob pointed out later that insects are always practicing.
Even the fast moving insects are always just doing what they do and fully doing it, fully immersed in each moment of their life.
So I really felt privileged to be part of this community, and immediately my practice was strengthened by my being there.
I felt like I was getting in touch with my true nature in a way that isn't possible in the human made world.
I was even tolerant of the gnats and flies and mosquitoes.
I recognized that they too are all part of this amazing, beautiful network of life.
I had already had some experience with mosquito practice from the previous evening of Zazen, as I think anybody else who sat outside probably has.
Their sustenance depends on blood and they're annoying, but the itch they leave behind is really a minor inconvenience if you think about it.
And probably these mountain mosquitoes are not likely to be carrying diseases.
So I let them land on my skin and feel that tiny prick as they insert their proboscis.
I actually felt some intimacy with them as they drink.
Think about that bond.
It's a pretty incredible thing.
Some of the mosquitoes though would land on my eyeball and others on the tip of my nose and others on my lips.
Those I would gently swish away.
I didn't glance at my watch much.
I just let my body dictate whether to sit or not.
After I grew tired of sitting, I would practice Kinhin in the meadow.
I had removed my boots and socks when I arrived, so I did this in bare feet, walking on the soft marshy earth, walking the length of huge fallen logs, walking through cold rocky creeks.
Sometimes on my walks I would discover new communities of life.
I would stop to observe them.
But eventually I would return to my spot and sit.
So there I was living in the meadow, and my comrades were having similar experiences in their solo spots, or maybe very different experiences.
But we were all doing this together and I was aware of that kinship.
As the sun slowly made its way around toward the west, I realized that Bob by now had collected my comrades from their solos.
Upon realizing this, I felt this sense of solitude for the first time.
I also felt a sense of fear being there alone in the meadow.
While walking in the meadow I had seen a pile of fresh bear scat, so I was aware that I wasn't the dominant species in this meadow.
And I contemplated the meaning of the line from the Heart Sutra that in the former translation was *the Bodhisattva depends on Prajnaparamita and the mind is no hindrance.
Without any hindrance no fears exist.*
I wondered if my practice was strong enough, if I could reach a point where no fears would exist.
I would just sit peacefully as a bear entered the meadow.
I wondered if my heart would even not race, if my practice was strong enough, as the bear approached and sniffed me up and down and then sat beside me and joined me in zazen.
So I tried harder to attain that depth of practice.
I sat with more intensity, and more and more mosquitoes began landing in my eyes.
By now I had dozens of mosquito bites on my face and hands and feet.
I found myself practicing with the first precept: *A disciple of Buddha does not take life.* I felt like I was under attack, and surely it's okay to kill if under attack.
I began to hate the mosquitoes.
And I questioned why I was even there.
Is it really necessary to retreat to the wilderness?
Couldn't I accomplish the same thing in the warmth and comfort of the zendo without the added discomfort of being out there suffering?
This sort of thinking made me question my identity, because for years, hiking and backpacking and climbing have been my primary practice.
I consider myself a person of nature.
So how could I be viewing nature in this negative light?
I found that my practice was clear when I was walking.
That was mostly because the mosquitoes didn't bother me while I was in motion.
So I did more of that in the afternoon.
I was fasting for the most part, but I did choose to eat fresh mountain blueberries because the earth had made them available in such abundance.
So I gobbled them up with gratitude.
I found that the highest concentration of life in the meadow was on the fallen logs, so I spent quite a bit of time there watching all the insects.
That's where I witnessed the mites.
These tiny red, spider-like creatures seemed to be engaged in battle.
At first I noticed two mites flailing their front legs around wildly, attacking each other.
Then I saw another mite attack the second one from the rear.
The attacked mite turned to face its new attacker, only to be attacked again from the rear by the first mite.
Then another mite joined in the fray.
It just became this incredible aggression.
Many mites against one mite until eventually they wore the one mite down.
I didn't witness the end of the battle, but I returned later and I found the attacked mite dead, alone there at the scene of the battle.
This had a huge impact on me.
Here I am sitting, hoping to end suffering in the world, imagining that humans are the problem and believing I can make a difference.
Now suddenly I feel like there's no hope.
If ruthless aggression and cruelty are innate at this level in nature, what hope is there really that we can ever change things?
As evening settled in, ominous clouds moved in, cutting me off from my view of the Sisters and Baker.
And it began to rain.
I retreated to my tent, which is tall enough that I can sort of sit inside.
My head presses into the ceiling.
I have to slouch as I sit, but it works in a pinch.
I sat with the problem of nature being inherently evil, and the rains fell harder and grew louder on my tent, and the creeks on both sides of me grew fuller and louder.

As I sat there, listening to the rain, I sensed how much the surrounding forest, the old growth trees and the bushes and the grasses and the mosses and all the sentient creatures appreciated that water.
It was cleansing and thirst-quenching.
Somehow the rain made everything okay.
It washes all the dirt away and it gives us a fresh start.
It's always done that, and it will always do that.
Sitting there listening to that rain, I somehow felt okay with the mites and okay with the world.
I glanced at my watch right at 9 o'clock, and I knew that in the valley below, my hiking companions were now chanting the Refuges in Pali, so I joined them.
I had thought I might sit into the night, but instead I decided to sleep, thinking maybe my dreams would bring a vision, something tangible that I could say I had learned on my solo.
I did, in fact, dream very actively that night, and one dream I remember vividly.
There was a bank robbery with alarms blaring and old school bank robbers fleeing the scene with black masks and carrying white bags with dollar signs on them.
There was a car chase after that.
Lots of explosions with a choreographed song and dance number.
And that final climactic scene took place on a basketball court.
I wasn't even a character in this dream, and there was nobody in it that I recognized.
It just seemed to have been presented to me solely for my entertainment.
When I woke up it was still raining, and I wondered what on earth I was supposed to do with that vision.
Two months later I'm still asking that question.
Maybe it means nothing.

I've come to believe, though, that it's telling me that life is like a Hollywood movie, with good guys and bad guys and adventure and plot twists and suffering and pleasure and maybe even happy endings.
And I think it was telling me to not take things too seriously as well, and to just enjoy the game.
By 7 a.m.
I had packed up my wet tent and was standing at the assigned trail junction when Bob arrived.
That was interesting, too.
He surprised me by arriving from a different direction than the one I expected.
It was like the [unclear: "champ book"].
I was facing the trail we had come up on and he came from this direction.
We exchanged a heartfelt gassho and he escorted me back to the group.
We finished a period of Zazen, had formal breakfast, talked a bit about my solo experience, and then we packed up and hiked out in the pouring rain.
That was the Mountains and Rivers retreat in 2010.
That's my talk.

We set up an altar inside. That's where we do most of our practice. And we settle in for evening zazen and kinen. And at the end of the day, under the glow of a single candle or maybe the moon or a blanket of stars or the faint red remnants of the sunset over the twin sisters' range, we chant the refuges in Pali. And I always get the sense that our voices are rising

up from that hut in the meadow, rising up into the mountains and sky and somehow bringing some relief or some benefit to someone, somewhere who desperately needs that. On Saturday morning, we arise. We have morning zazen, a formal silent breakfast. And then Bob leads each one of us to various sites that he's selected for our solos. And for the rest of the morning, which I believe is about two to three hours, we have time and space, each of us, to be alone with nature. And this year, for the first time, Bob invited me to do an extended solo. So

when the traditional two to three hour solo had ended, Bob made the rounds and picked up each person, escorted them back to the zendo and the meadow. And they sat another round of zazen, had lunch, then broke silence and had an informal afternoon for day hiking. Usually during that time, we either go up to the fire lookout on Park Butte or over to the railroad grade, just a glacier moraine looking out over the south side of Mount Baker. And this year I understand that you guys opted for Park Butte. And then the group returns for an informal dinner, followed by regular

evening practice, ending again with the refuges and poly. So this year, while my comrades were doing all this, I remained at my solo site roughly 24 hours until Bob returned to pick me up after the group's first period of morning zazen on Sunday morning. So what happened during my solo? This is the part where I just sit. Well, going in, I sort of wondered what to expect. I considered for a while whether or should I should try to attain something or do anything special in my practice at all. And I talked to Tim about that. I talked to Bob about that. But

generally, we all sort of agreed that it's probably best to expect nothing. And I considered my return as well. When I came down from the mountain to join the group, what was that experience going to be like? I knew there was time allocated to talk about what I had just experienced. I sort of imagined that I would be glowing. You know, Charlton Heston has a new hairstyle when he comes down off of the mountain. That wasn't going to happen. Or maybe I would just come back and report that nothing had happened. Well, I wouldn't say that nothing happened in my spot. Maybe

superficially, if I hadn't been paying attention, I might describe the scene there as nothing. It was just a silent meadow. There really wasn't anything spectacular happening there. There was nothing to do there. It was, however, quite a meadow. Bob has a real knack for picking spots. There were several small creeks meandering through it. To the west, I had a great view of the Sisters and to the northwest, the Black Buttes. On all other sides, my meadow was surrounded by a thin ribbon of forest then talus fields expanding upward toward some pretty spectacular cliff

faces. This year we had a more or less constant threat of rain. So the first thing I did was find some relatively high flat ground to pitch a tent, just in case it was needed. Then I found a spot in the meadow near the junction of two creeks and I sat and watched and listened. And almost immediately I discovered that this was no quiet meadow. Right in front of me there was constant motion. Dozens, maybe hundreds of species of insects all scurrying or flying around, some fast, some slow. Some, like ants and beetles, seemed to be on a mission in a frantic hurry to get somewhere. While

others, like a lone bee and a lone spider and another flying insect with long narrow wings and long antennae that I couldn't identify, seemed to be joining me in Zazen. They just sat there for a very long time with me and I really felt like they were aware that I was practicing Zazen and they were joining me in that practice. Bob pointed out later that insects are always practicing, even the fast moving insects are always just doing what they do and fully doing it, fully immersed in each moment of their life. So I really felt privileged to be part of this community and

immediately my practice was strengthened by my being there. I felt like I was getting in touch with my true nature in a way that isn't possible in the human made world. I was even tolerant of the gnats and flies and mosquitoes. I recognized that they too are all part of this amazing, beautiful network of life. And I had already had some experience with mosquito practice from the previous evening of Zazen, as I think anybody else who sat outside probably has. Their sustenance depends on blood and they're annoying, but the itch they leave behind is really a

minor inconvenience if you think about it. And probably these mountain mosquitoes are not likely to be carrying diseases. So I let them land on my skin and feel that tiny prick as they insert their proboscis. And I actually felt some intimacy with them as they drink. Think about that bond. It's a pretty incredible thing. Some of the mosquitoes though would land on my eyeball and others on the tip of my nose and others on my lips. And those I would gently swish away. I didn't glance at my watch much. Just let my body dictate whether to sit or not.

After I grew tired of sitting, I would practice Kinhin in the meadow. I had removed my boots and socks when I arrived, so I did this in bare feet, walking on the soft marshy earth, walking the length of huge fallen logs, walking through cold rocky creeks. And sometimes on my walks I would discover new communities of life. I would stop to observe them. But eventually I would return to my spot and sit. So there I was living in the meadow and having similar experiences in their solo spots or maybe very different experiences. But we were all doing this together

and I was aware of that kinship. And as the sun slowly made its way around toward the west, I realized that Bob by now had collected my comrades from their solos. And upon realizing this, I felt this sense of solitude for the first time. I also felt a sense of fear being there alone in the meadow. While walking in the meadow I had seen a pile of fresh bear scat. So I was aware that I wasn't the dominant species in this meadow. And I contemplated the meaning of the line from the Heart Sutra

that in the former translation was the Bodhisattva depends on Prajnaparamita and the mind is no hindrance. Without any hindrance no fears exist. And I wondered if my practice was strong enough if I could reach a point where no fears would exist. And I would just sit peacefully as a bear entered the meadow. I wondered if my heart would even not race if my practice was strong enough. As the bear approached and sniffed me up and down and then sat beside me and joined me in zazen. So I tried

harder to attain that depth of practice. I sat with more intensity and more and more mosquitoes began landing in my eyes. By now I had dozens of mosquito bites on my face and hands and feet. And I found myself practicing with the first precept. A disciple of Buddha does not take life. I felt like I was under attack. And surely it's okay to kill if under attack. I began to hate the mosquitoes. And I questioned why I was even there. Is it really necessary to retreat to the

wilderness? Couldn't I accomplish the same thing in the warmth and comfort of the zendo without the added discomfort of being out there suffering? This sort of thinking made me question my identity. Because for years, hiking and backpacking and climbing have been my primary practice. And I consider myself a person of nature. So how could I be viewing nature in this negative light? I found that my practice was clear when I was walking. That was mostly because the mosquitoes didn't bother me while I was in motion.

So I did more of that in the afternoon. I was fasting for the most part, but I did choose to eat fresh mountain blueberries because the earth had made them available in such abundance. So I gobbled them up with gratitude. I found that the highest concentration of life in the meadow was on the fallen logs. So I spent quite a bit of time there watching all the insects. And that's where I witnessed the mites. These tiny red, spider-like creatures seem to be engaged in battle. At first I noticed two mites

flailing their front legs around wildly attacking each other. Then I saw another mite attack the second one from the rear. The attacked mite turned to face its new attacker, only to be attacked again from the rear by the first mite. And then another mite joined in the fray. It just became this incredible aggression. Many mites against one mite until eventually they wore the one mite down. I didn't witness the end of the battle, but I returned later and I found the attacked mite dead alone there at the scene of the battle.

And this had a huge impact on me. Here I am sitting hoping to end suffering in the world, imagining that humans are the problem and believing I can make a difference. Now suddenly I sort of feel like there's no hope. If ruthless aggression and cruelty are innate at this level in nature, what hope is there really that we can ever change things? As evening settled in, ominous clouds moved in, cutting me off from my view of the sisters in black boots. And it began to rain. I retreated to my tent, which is tall enough that I can

sort of sit inside. My head presses into the ceiling. I sort of have to slouch as I sit, but it works in a pinch. I sat with the problem of nature being inherently evil, and the rains fell harder and grew louder on my tent. And the creeks on both sides of me grew fuller and louder. And as I sat there, listening to the rain, I sensed how much the surrounding forest, the old growth trees and the bushes and the grasses and the mosses and all the sentient creatures appreciated that water.

It was cleansing and thirst-clenching. And somehow the rain made everything okay. It washes all the dirt away and it gives us a fresh start. It's always done that, and it will always do that. And sitting there listening to that rain, I somehow felt okay with the mites and okay with the world. I glance at my watch right at 9 o'clock, and I knew that in the valley below, my hiking companions were now chanting the Refuge and Refugees in Pali, so I joined them. And I had thought I might sit into the night,

but instead I decided to sleep, thinking maybe my dreams would bring a vision. Something tangible that I could say I had learned on my solo. I did, in fact, dream very actively that night. And one dream I remember vividly. There was a bank robbery with alarms blaring and old school bank robbers fleeing the scene with black masks and carrying white bags with dollar signs on them. And there was a car chase after that. Lots of explosions with a choreographed song and dance number.

And that final climactic scene took place on a basketball court. I wasn't even a character in this dream. And there was nobody in it that I recognized. It just seemed to have been presented to me solely for my entertainment. When I woke up it was still raining, and I wondered what on earth I was supposed to do with that vision. Two months later I'm still asking that question. Maybe it means nothing. I've come to believe, though, that it's telling me that life is like a Hollywood movie, with good guys and bad guys

and adventure and plot twists and suffering and pleasure and maybe even happy endings. And I think it was telling me to not take things too seriously as well and to just enjoy the game. By 7 a.m. I had packed up my wet tent and was standing at the assigned trail junction when Bob arrived. That was kind of interesting, too. He surprised me by arriving from a different direction than the one I expected. It was kind of like the champ book. I was facing the trail we had come up on and he came from this direction.

We exchanged a heartfelt cashew and he escorted me back to the group. We finished a period of Zazen, had formal breakfast, talked a bit about my solo experience, and then we packed up and hiked out in the pouring rain. That was the Mountains and Rivers retreat in 2010. That's my talk.
